extracted.intended_audience: Wikipedia editors and contributors (people deciding whether to create or keep Wikipedia articles about news events)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for deciding whether events or news items merit a standalone Wikipedia article versus merging, deletion, or placement on Wikinews; focuses on notability, verifiability, sources, and long‑term encyclopedic value. Useful to editors evaluating current events and news-derived topics for inclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encyclopedic requirement: significant lasting and historical interest and impact
rubrics_metrics.description: "Articles about items in the news are only considered encyclopedic if they are verifiably of significant lasting and historical interest and impact.",
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a crime that led to significant change in the law; an event that became a sensation; a death that led to new safety practices. If an event’s importance is only transitory, it likely does not merit a standalone article.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclude events of strictly passing significance
rubrics_metrics.description: "Articles should not be about events that have strictly passing significance and interest.",
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such subjects are likely only useful for a short time and should be considered for deletion or merger into a broader related article (for example, merge a one‑shot celebrity news item into the celebrity's main article). Exercise caution, but prefer merging or deletion for clearly ephemeral events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement for independent secondary documentation/analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: "The subject of the news item has become the subject of secondary documentation or analysis independent of news services. This includes being the subject of books, documentaries or non-trivial academic study (i.e. excluding non-scientific surveys).",
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Secondary sources and independent analysis are strong indicators of encyclopedic value. Mere repeated news reports without independent scholarly or in‑depth coverage are weaker evidence of notability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precedent/impact criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: "The subject of the news item has set, or has caused to set, a precedent in some way. This includes new laws being passed, novel interpretations of existing law, first tests of new law, notable 'first of its kind' achievements, new or increased safety legislation, causing a notable change in societal behaviour or norms, etc.",
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concrete, demonstrable changes in law, policy, or social behavior are grounds for inclusion. Note: "Predictions that it will set a precedent, however, are inappropriate attempts to predict the future." Do not rely on speculative future impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sustained and follow-up coverage indicates notability
rubrics_metrics.description: "Subjects which have already received significant coverage over a period of time, with follow-up stories exploring new information or story angles are demonstrably not of only one-time interest.",
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ongoing reporting and new angles over time support creating a standalone article; a single-day spike of coverage does not.

rubrics_metrics.name: Single-wire/press-release duplication rule for sources
rubrics_metrics.description: "Where a single news wire story or press release has been used by several news publications, this should only be counted as a single source in all notability discussions. Likewise, when reporters base their information off other news coverage (for example, 'AP reported that ...'), the coverage is only a single source.",
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derivative reports are not independent and cannot verify each other. Conversely, independent reporting by multiple mainstream outlets counts as multiple sources and strengthens notability.

rubrics_metrics.name: No original reporting on Wikipedia; use Wikinews for original/current reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: "For those who wish to write about current events... our sister project, Wikinews is specifically intended to cover current events, and also permits original reporting that is not allowed on Wikipedia.",
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a topic is of dubious encyclopedic value now, consider drafting it on Wikinews and adding sources there as the story develops. If reliable secondary sources later support encyclopedic inclusion, a Wikipedia article can be developed using those sources — but exclude original reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Merge rather than create stand-alone article when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: "News items that do not meet the above criteria, but which involve a notable subject should be included in the article about the notable subject, if it can be put in appropriate context there.",
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If no single subject is an appropriate merge target, consider creating a stand‑alone article only after adding additional material to appropriately contextualize the content. Avoid fragmentary, context‑less stubs about transient events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Routine news coverage is not a sufficient basis for inclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: "routine news coverage of announcements, events, sports, or celebrities, while sometimes useful, is not by itself a sufficient basis for inclusion of the subject of that coverage" (cited from WP:NOT#NEWS).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors should not equate routine newsworthiness with encyclopedic notability. Repeated routine coverage does not automatically justify a standalone encyclopedia article.

rubrics_metrics.name: Core application of verifiability, notability, and reliable sources
rubrics_metrics.description: The essay emphasizes application of the standard Wikipedia guidelines: verifiability, notability, and reliable sources (noted as the baseline criteria that would, if applied literally, permit many news events).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply these core policies when assessing news topics, but recognize practical editorial judgement: strict literal application could permit trivial topics; weigh long‑term significance and independent analysis rather than mere contemporaneous reporting.
